page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The critical temperature Tc of a gas is the
highest temperature at which the gas can be
Above Tc no amount of pressure can liquefy
steps.why: Liquefaction needs the intermolecular attractions to hold the molecules together. Above the critical temperature the molecular kinetic energy is too large for that, so pressure alone can no longer produce a liquid.
common_mistakes: Writing lowest temperature instead of highest. Tc is the upper limit for liquefaction by pressure.
Leaving out by applying pressure — cooling alone is a different route.
steps.memory_tip: Tc is the maximum temperature for liquefying by pressure: at or below it pressure can liquefy the gas, above it pressure cannot.
steps.margin_note: Both sentences together make the definition exact: the limit, and what fails above it.

steps.label: The value for CO₂
lines: Below 31.1 °C, CO₂ gas can be liquefied by
steps.why: CO₂ is the textbook example because its critical temperature sits just above room temperature, which is why CO₂ cylinders and fire extinguishers can hold liquid CO₂ under pressure.
common_mistakes: Quoting 31.1 K instead of 31.1 °C. The value is in degrees Celsius.
Rounding to 31 °C is accepted; swapping digits to 13.1 is not.
steps.memory_tip: 31.1 °C — just above a hot summer day. That is why liquid CO₂ exists in cylinders at room temperature.
steps.margin_note: The Celsius value is the expected answer; the kelvin form in brackets is extra.

insider_note: The word highest is what the examiner underlines — a definition that reads as a lowest temperature is marked wrong even with the correct CO₂ value beside it.
